45.bp: Cities need to know what will happen in every neighborhood: Will this area need more police? More doctors? Where should we build affordable housing? Urban planners need dozens of predictions at once, from crime to air quality to transportation patterns, and these things are deeply tangled together—fixing one often changes another.
45.wh: Most systems predict one thing at a time: crime separately from traffic, hospitals separately from restaurants. This misses how everything in a city connects. Also, there's no fair way to compare different approaches because everyone uses different test data and different neighborhoods, so you can't tell if one method actually works better or just got lucky.

The approach uses a Mixture-of-Experts architecture, which works like having specialized teams of data analysts instead of one generalist. Each team is trained to look at certain types of input signals (traffic cameras, weather, census data) and make predictions for the indicators it's best at. A router mechanism decides which features go to which expert.
45.ww: When you let specialists focus on what they do best, you save computation and get better predictions—a doctor shouldn't diagnose broken bones if they're a cardiologist. Here, different neighborhoods and their data patterns are handled by different experts, and the system only uses the computation it actually needs instead of wasting resources on every possible path.
45.po: On real data from three cities, UrbanMoE predicted multiple urban outcomes simultaneously better than all other methods tested. It makes planning faster too—fewer calculations mean planners get answers sooner when they need to make decisions.

46.bp: We used to think the main threat from AI-generated fake media was the shocking deepfake videos—a celebrity's face pasted onto someone else's body. But now that AI can generate tons of text automatically, the real danger is subtler and bigger: thousands of articles that sound plausible get created and spread, making people unsure what's even true anymore.
46.wh: Videos are visceral and memorable—one deepfake video can alarm millions. But text is scalable: one AI can pump out articles by the thousands, slowly poisoning the information ecosystem until no one trusts anything. The hard part isn't spotting an obvious fake; it's noticing when real-looking text has been synthetically manufactured at scale.
46.ap: Researchers interviewed 21 experts across AI, policy, and misinformation—asking them how serious different kinds of AI fakes are and which defense strategies work. They then asked about the measurement problem: how do you even *count* if your defense is working when there's no standard way to test it?
46.ww: When you talk to people who've fought this before, they tell you what actually matters. Experts said technical tools (like classifiers that try to spot fakes) don't work as well as everyone hoped, but clear rules about where information comes from—provenance standards—do. You need reproducible methods so when someone claims a defense works, others can verify it independently.
46.po: The researchers found that treating information integrity like infrastructure—requiring proof of where things came from, documenting methods rigorously—is what actually stops synthetic consensus from forming. Without that, fake media spreads faster than detection catches up.

47.bp: When a large organization wants to train a machine learning model using data from branches in different countries or departments, they face a privacy problem: they can't just send raw patient records or transaction logs to a central server. Federated Learning lets each branch train its own model locally, then share only the learned patterns, keeping raw data private. But now imagine each branch has different needs—a rural clinic serves different patients than an urban hospital.
47.wh: In federated learning, the central server collects what each branch's model learned and merges those learnings together. But merging creates a tug-of-war: the merged model gets good at the common patterns across all branches but bad at what makes each branch unique. Each branch then tries to improve locally, but that pulls it back toward its own old habits. You end up with something that's mediocre everywhere.
47.ap: Thorki gives each branch two models instead of one: a small personal model for its unique patients, and a large shared model for general patterns. When making a decision, a fusion network (a lightweight model that learns to blend predictions) takes predictions from both and combines them. The small model and large model never directly compete—they cooperate through the fusion network's learned weights.
47.ww: By splitting the job of learning into two separate models, Thorki stops the general and personal from fighting each other. The small model never has to forget how to help unique patients, and the large model can become a true general expert without being pulled back by local oddities. When both answer and are combined thoughtfully, you get better results from each branch.
47.po: On real hospital and business data, Thorki was 0.16% to 19% more accurate than other federated systems, and trained to good accuracy 2 to 10 times faster. Each branch gets to keep its specialized knowledge while also benefiting from learning across the entire organization.

48.bp: On streaming platforms like Twitch, thousands of viewers chat at once. Moderators have to catch insults, threats, and harassment instantly. But these happen at scale and speed no human team can match, while also facing abuse themselves. We need AI to help filter the toxic stuff before it spreads.
48.wh: Standard keyword filtering catches obvious curses but misses insults hidden in slang. A word by itself might be innocent, but next to other words becomes cruel. Also, Twitch is unique—people send emotes (little cartoon faces and icons) mixed into their messages, and those emotes carry meaning. A message "you suck" alone is rude, but "you suck [laughing emoji]" might be joking with friends. Most AI systems completely ignore emotes.
48.ap: ToxiTwitch combines several tools: it takes the text message and turns it into numbers (using recent large language models), separately turns the emotes into numbers, then feeds both into traditional machine learning classifiers (Random Forest and SVM) that learned from labeled examples of toxic and non-toxic Twitch messages. The classifiers say yes or no based on both the text and the emote signals together.
48.ww: Emotes are context—they tell you the intent behind the words. When you include context, you make fewer mistakes. A random forest or SVM can learn patterns: "this type of word + this type of emoji = usually joking, don't flag it," whereas ignoring emotes forces the system to guess without half the information.
48.po: When trained on one specific channel's message history, ToxiTwitch caught toxic behavior with 80% accuracy, beating a standard AI model (BERT) by 13 percentage points. It flagged 76% of the toxic messages it found (the precision measure), meaning fewer false alarms that misdirect moderator attention.

49.bp: Large language models train on billions of pages from the internet. Some of those pages contain sensitive information: medical records that were publicly posted by mistake, private emails someone published, confidential documents. The question is: did the model memorize that sensitive stuff? If it did, an attacker might be able to trick it into repeating your private data back to them.
49.wh: Testing for memorization is tricky because AI models often learn the *meaning* of something without learning the exact words. You could feed the model "John Smith had diabetes" and then try "john smith has diabetes" (different grammar, same meaning) and it might not recognize it as the same—so a naive test would think the model didn't memorize the original, when it actually did.
49.ap: ASMIA takes a potential secret from the training data and creates multiple versions that mean the same thing but sound different—like paraphrasing a sentence. It shows all these versions to the model and watches the attention patterns (where the model's focus goes when processing). It then builds a classifier that learns the difference between the model's response to information it trained on versus random new information, using both the model's confidence numbers and the attention patterns.
49.ww: Attention patterns reveal understanding—if a model truly learned something deeply, it will pay attention to it in consistent ways regardless of paraphrasing. By checking many semantically equivalent versions, you catch memorization that word-for-word matching would miss. A smart classifier trained on these signals can spot the difference between genuine knowledge and random guessing.
49.po: On Wikipedia (a large real corpus), ASMIA detected training data leakage far better than existing methods. It shows that models do memorize sensitive patterns, even when those patterns are reworded, confirming a real privacy risk that simpler tests would have missed.

50.bp: DiDi and Uber predict ride demand by neighborhood and time so they can position drivers efficiently: surge pricing when demand is high, surge pricing areas to incentivize drivers, and planning where to hire more drivers. Accurate forecasts mean riders wait less, drivers earn more, and the system stays balanced. Poor forecasts mean wasted driver time and frustrated passengers.
50.wh: Cities are complex—the same intersection behaves wildly differently during a concert, a rainstorm, or a traffic jam. Raw historical data doesn't contain the semantics: a data point says "100 rides picked up here at 3pm" but doesn't explain why. Also, different neighborhoods have different personalities: a business district at 9am versus a nightlife district at 9pm are completely different prediction problems.
50.ap: MVGR-Net learns neighborhood personality in a pre-training stage by looking at two things: the types of places nearby (restaurants, offices, parks—semantic attributes that give character) and actual movement patterns from historical trips. This creates a rich numeric sketch of each neighborhood. Later, when forecasting, it fine-tunes a large language model on this sketch, feeding in details about external events (concerts, weather) as context.
50.ww: By understanding neighborhood character first, you know what to expect: office areas have predictable morning spikes, tourist areas spike at different times. When you then add information about specific events happening today, the model understands how those events *alter* normal patterns rather than trying to learn from scratch each time. Geospatial understanding plus event context is far more powerful than either alone.
50.po: On DiDi's real forecasting task, MVGR-Net achieved state-of-the-art performance, meaning it predicted rider demand more accurately than competing approaches, enabling more efficient driver dispatch and fewer empty rides.

51.bp: Drug discovery works like this: researchers design a molecule, test it, measure how well it works (does it kill cancer cells? is it toxic?). To speed this up, AI can propose new molecules. But the AI trains on old data of molecules that worked. Then a pharmaceutical company wants it to discover molecules for a *new* disease where the rules might be different—will it still work?
51.wh: A molecule's effectiveness comes from its structure plus the disease being treated. The AI mixes these two together in one mathematical space. When the disease changes (new distribution), the learned pattern breaks because the model relied on correlations specific to the old disease. For example, a feature that predicted success in cancer might be irrelevant or even harmful in Alzheimer's.
51.ap: MoFE builds a graph neural network that explicitly separates the unchanging structural rules (these atoms bonded this way always act this way) from the changeable rules (how that structure helps *this specific* disease). It adds a Mixture-of-Experts layer where different expert networks specialize in different structural patterns. When you describe a new editing goal, the system routes through the expert best suited to that structure and disease combination.
51.ww: By keeping invariant principles (physics) separate from variant details (disease-specific effects), the model can swap in new disease contexts and still get the physics right. Each expert learns to focus on one aspect, so when the disease changes, the experts' core understanding of structure stays valid—only the high-level routing needs to adjust.
51.po: MoFE designed molecules that were more effective across different diseases and instruction types than models that didn't separate invariant and variant factors, suggesting it could be more useful for discovering drugs when the disease domain changes.

52.bp: Imagine you sketch a rough drawing of a bird and want to find photos of birds that match your sketch. The challenge: your sketch is crude and abstract—just curved lines—while real bird photos are detailed. A human would mentally interpret the sketch and look for photos with those visual traits. We want AI to do the same.
52.wh: Sketches are missing information—no colors, no fine details, no background. A naive approach tries to find mathematical patterns that connect sketches directly to photos, but there's a huge gap to bridge. Convolutional networks and distance learning (trying to make similar sketches and images close together numerically) can work, but they miss what the sketch is actually *about*—the semantic intention behind the artist's lines.
52.ap: SketchMind uses a multimodal large language model to look at the sketch and describe what it *means* using text (like a person explaining their drawing). Then it builds a graph where the sketch is in the center and multiple text descriptions are nodes around it. A graph attention mechanism (learned weights on connections) decides which descriptions are reliable and which are noise, then blends them together. Finally, a Jigsaw Matching module finds local and global visual correspondences between the sketch's refined meaning and candidate photos.
52.ww: Language is precise where sketches are ambiguous. A language model can say "this looks like a hummingbird with flowers," which narrows the search enormously. By using attention on the graph, the system learns to trust key descriptions and ignore spurious details. Then you can match both fine details (the flowers' shape) and the overall scene, so you find the right photo even when it's photographed from a different angle or lighting.
52.po: SketchMind retrieved the correct images more reliably than existing systems that didn't use language understanding, showing that language-aware reasoning helps bridge the abstraction gap between rough sketches and detailed photos.

53.bp: Blockchain systems like Bitcoin are slow when they try to run on one computer. Sharding splits the workload: each shard is a mini-blockchain handling a portion of transactions. If 16 shards work in parallel, you should get roughly 16x speed. But reality is messier: transactions often reference data from multiple shards, causing shards to block and wait for each other.
53.wh: Without coordination, each shard schedules transactions independently. This leads to conflicts: shard A packages a transaction that depends on data from shard B, but shard B hasn't processed its part yet. They block each other. Centralized coordination eliminates conflicts but adds a bottleneck and a security risk—one coordinator could cheat. You need coordination that's both decentralized and conflict-free.
53.ap: Concordia lets each shard predict future cross-shard interactions using a Graph Neural Network—basically, each shard learns patterns in who transacts with whom and predicts which transactions will soon need data from other shards. Shards then broadcast these predictions to each other (small messages, not full data). Each shard uses this hint to pack its transactions better: it delays those that will conflict and confirms those that won't.
53.ww: Prediction prevents conflicts rather than resolving them after they happen. If a shard knows "these transactions will need input from shard B," it can schedule them intelligently—group them or defer them. Graph neural networks are good at learning patterns from interconnected data, so they're natural for predicting transaction dependencies. Broadcasting lightweight signals keeps the system decentralized without the overhead of sharing full data.
53.po: On a 16-shard system, Concordia doubled throughput and dropped conflicts from 62% to 1.5%, and was 1.67x faster than a centralized scheduler while reducing communication overhead by 95%, showing that cooperative prediction works better than either independent or centralized approaches.

54.bp: When you ask an AI assistant a question and it responds with text, it goes through many intermediate steps. At each step, the model is uncertain and picks the token it thinks is most likely. But sometimes the model focuses too hard on simple filler words (like "the" or "a") instead of the conceptually important words. This is called an attention sink. It's like a student who memorizes the pronoun "the" so well they stop learning anything else.
54.wh: Existing fixes try to either block these filler words or redistribute attention mechanically. But this breaks the meaning—if you block "the," the whole sentence falls apart. A principled fix should let filler words exist but reduce their dominance while keeping meaning intact. The tension: you want to stay faithful to semantics while also removing noise.
54.ap: PAOSC uses two neural networks: a generator that looks at the model's processing and flags which tokens are informationally important, and a discriminator that trains the generator using policy gradient methods (essentially reinforcement learning). The training signal comes from measuring whether the model's confidence stayed stable and whether the loss changed when that token was kept or dropped.
54.ww: Measuring information by confidence and loss changes directly approximates importance—if dropping a token hardly changes the model's behavior, it's probably not carrying meaning. Policy gradients let you optimize this without needing labeled data saying "this token is important." The generator learns by trial: trying different masks and seeing which ones preserve meaning best.
54.po: On eight different language models, PAOSC improved accuracy scores by up to 9.68%. On a constructed dataset, it identified and eliminated 18% of low-value tokens, making inference faster while keeping quality intact.

55.bp: Online retailers recommend what you might buy next based on your recent browsing: you looked at running shoes, so we show you socks. This is session-based recommendation—using short sequences of clicks to predict the next item. The challenge is scale: millions of sessions, and every person who looked at running shoes shouldn't get the exact same recommendation.
55.wh: When two shoppers' sessions end with the same last item (both looked at socks), the algorithm tends to give them identical predictions next—both get shoe recommendations. But they're different people with different history; the one who was browsing winter clothes should see cold-weather items, not the one browsing summer wear. Graph neural networks learned to model session sequences, but they inherit this flaw. Also, popular items (bestsellers) get recommended too often just because they appear in many sessions.
55.ap: SAGE builds a graph of all items and connections (what sequences naturally occur). Then, for each session, it creates multiple versions: one with random variations to act as positive examples and another with negative examples from unpopular items. Using contrastive learning, the system learns to make the session embedding (the numeric summary) match positive variations while staying different from negative ones. This trains the system to distinguish sessions that superficially look similar.
55.ww: Contrastive learning teaches by comparing: "this session is similar to that variation but different from this unrelated session." By creating intentional variations and negatives, you force the model to learn what's unique about each session beyond just the last item. The popularity bias correction (using negative samples from unpopular items) rebalances the recommendation: rare items get a fair chance.
55.po: When SAGE was combined with various existing graph-based systems, all of them improved—especially better at distinguishing sessions with the same last item, showing that the approach generalizes across different architectures and helps systems recommend more diverse and personalized items.

56.bp: Your phone has a small AI model running on it to transcribe speech or suggest completions—no internet required, your data stays private. But personalizing that model (making it better at your accent or your vocabulary) means either uploading your data to the cloud or fine-tuning on-device. Both have costs: cloud annotations are expensive, and fine-tuning drains the phone's battery and storage.
56.wh: The obvious solution—have the cloud service annotate all your data—is expensive. The other extreme—download a big model and fine-tune everything locally—wastes power and memory. You need a middle ground where you're selective about which data to annotate and which model layers to actually change, so the process is cheap and efficient.
56.ap: EcoTune uses a multi-armed bandit strategy (a classic algorithm for deciding what to try next) to identify the highest-value user interactions—messages that would teach the model the most if they were labeled. Only those go to the cloud for annotation. Meanwhile, for on-device tuning, it analyzes which model layers matter most (using layer importance scores) and only updates those layers, leaving the rest frozen.
56.ww: Selective annotation saves money—you annotate the 20% of data that teaches 80% of what the model needs to know. Selective layer updates save memory and power—unfreezing everything means computing gradients everywhere, but if only 20% of the model matters for your specific use case, you waste 80% of the compute. Both selectivity decisions compound to make personalization cheap.
56.po: On real devices, EcoTune needed 20% to 60% fewer annotations than baseline methods and significantly cut the memory required for fine-tuning, making on-device personalization practical even with small budgets.

57.bp: When an e-commerce site recommends items, it uses many signals: clicks (you looked at it), carts (you wanted it), and purchases (you bought it). Clicks are the noisiest—someone might click out of curiosity or by accident. Purchases are the clearest signal of actual interest. Mixing all these together is tricky: the noisy signals can confuse the model into learning bad patterns.
57.wh: If you naively combine all signals equally, clicks overwhelm the model (there are thousands of clicks for every purchase), and the noise in clicks teaches the model bad preferences. If you weight purchases heavily, you ignore useful hints from clicks. The core issue: different users care about auxiliary behaviors differently, and those patterns shift over time or between product categories—it's not stable.
57.ap: RMBRec uses two modules working in parallel. The Representation Robustness Module maximizes how much the model's internal representation of a user from clicks matches their representation from purchases (high mutual information)—this purifies representations by only keeping the user preferences that are truly consistent. The Optimization Robustness Module minimizes the variance of prediction errors across different behavior types—if the model does well on clicks but poorly on purchases, that variance is high, and the module penalizes it.
57.ww: Consistency signals truth—if a user's preferences from clicks and purchases are similar, that's real preference. By maximizing this consistency, you separate signal from noise. Reducing variance across behaviors stabilizes learning: instead of fitting one behavior perfectly and failing on others, you learn a robust model that works across all of them. Both together create a representation that's meaningful rather than just fitting noise.
57.po: On three real e-commerce datasets, RMBRec improved prediction accuracy, especially on the target purchase behavior, while being more robust to the noise and inconsistency in auxiliary behaviors like clicks.

58.bp: Researchers build separate AI systems for graphs from different domains: social networks predict friendships, molecule graphs predict chemical properties, recommendation graphs predict products you'll buy. Each system trains from scratch. The question: can we pre-train on *all* graphs together and build a general-purpose system that works across domains?
58.wh: Graphs vary wildly: a social network's nodes are people, a molecule graph's nodes are atoms. Their meanings are completely different, so a system trained on one doesn't directly transfer to another. Naive approaches treat all graphs identically, which fails—they're asking a model to learn from apples and oranges together without understanding what makes each fruit unique.
58.ap: LEDA first maps all graphs into a shared semantic space using a dimension projection unit (learned transformations that adapt each graph's features without losing information). Then, a variational semantic inference module (a probabilistic model) learns a shared latent distribution—a statistical description of patterns that show up across domains. Pre-training objectives then use this distribution to guide learning, making sure the model captures cross-domain insights.
58.ww: By mapping into a shared space before learning, you're saying: "underneath their surface differences, all these graphs share structural patterns." A variational distribution captures the common structure. Pre-training with this distribution as guidance teaches the model to look for these universal patterns instead of memorizing domain-specific quirks. When you then apply the pre-trained model to a new domain, it starts with universal understanding rather than random initialization.
58.po: LEDA improved performance on downstream graph tasks across multiple domains compared to training separate models or using simple pre-training approaches, showing that learning universal principles across diverse graphs makes the system more useful for new domains.

59.bp: On social media and video platforms, false information spreads fast. A video with misleading audio or edited images can fool millions. Detecting fake videos requires checking: is this video of a real event, or is it fabricated? We need to look both at what the video contains and at information from outside sources to verify it.
59.wh: Inside the video, you only have images, sound, and text—no ground truth. A fake video can be well-made and convincing. To check if it's really fake, you need external context: was this event reported in real news? Do reference videos of the same event exist? But combining external knowledge with internal signals is complex—you have to understand what each signal means and how they relate.
59.ap: TrueLens works in two layers. Externally, it breaks the video into text, visual, and audio components, uses a multimodal language model to describe each one, then retrieves similar videos from a database of known real and fake examples—it finds one real reference and one fake reference. The Adversarial Contrastor compares the query video with both references, learning what makes it similar to or different from each. Internally, the Evidential Logic Fusion module combines signals from text, images, and audio to make a final judgment.
59.ww: Reference videos ground your decision: if this video matches patterns from known fakes, it's probably fake. If it matches real videos, it's probably real. The contrastive comparison (what's like the fake reference? what's like the real reference?) is more informative than absolute judgments. Fusing multiple modalities internally catches fakes that fool one modality but are caught by another—a deepfake video might look real but have weird audio patterns.
59.po: On three benchmark datasets, TrueLens outperformed competing systems at distinguishing real from fake videos, and remained robust when the temporal patterns or event types in test data differed from training, showing that reference-based reasoning generalizes.
